item.title: Rattlesnake Lodge to Folk Art Center along the MST 10 miles, 1400' elevation — Wed Oct 14, 8:00 AM
item.description:
The Asheville Hiking Group **Meeting Spot**: Folk Art Center on the Blue Ridge Parkway. Prompt 8:00 departure **Description**: This is a point to point hike. We will meet at the Folk Art Center and shuttle up to the Rattle Snake Lodge starting point. Follow the MST Trail from the remnants of the Rattlesnake Lodge, a turn of the century lodge built by an Asheville physician, to the Folk Art Center. There is a large variety of colorful wildflowers along the trail, which is mostly downhill with a few short climbs. There is a nice overlook for a lunch/snack break. Good footing. Shaded. Pace: 2.4 mph. Dogs welcome if on a leash. **Please Note:** This is a longer hike than my usual. If it's a warm day, I recommend bringing along extra water.
**Courtesy, (Please Abide!)**

item.title: "Lost Ground: America's Landslide Crisis" Film Screening — Wed Oct 14, 6:30 PM
item.description:
UNC Asheville will be screening the recent documentary “Lost Ground: America’s Landslide Crisis” in Mullen & James Humanities Hall. The screening is to be followed by a panel discussion and Q&A moderated by the director, WCNC’s investigative reporter Nate Morabito. The panelists include:
Paige Ambord and Caitlin Meagher, faculty in the Department of Sociology and Anthropology and who are featured in the film for their work on landslide survivors post-Helene Jackie Langille, an expert on landslide geography in the Department of Environmental Science.
This important film exposes the extent of landslide damage during Helene, and raises awareness of landslide risks, two years after that devastating event.

item.title: Rice Pinnacle Lollipop: 5.3 mi., 530 ft. Elev. Gain — Fri Oct 16, 9:00 AM
item.description:
The Asheville Hiking Group **[Sign-up opens 8:00 PM, Sunday October 11th]**
**Please read the carpool info below the hike description.**
This is a typical lovely hike in the Bent Creek area. It incorporates segments from the Wolf Branch and Corvair Trails, along with several connectors. At 5.3 miles and a tame 530' elevation gain, I'd rate it 2.5 on a 0-10 difficulty scale. We'll average around 2.4 mph -- not a fitness hike, but you should have enough experience hiking to know you can deal with mild hills and a moderate pace.
We'll stop for a brief snack & water break halfway around. Wear sensible hiking boots. If you're on the fence about hiking poles, you probably don't need them for this one.
***Dog Policy:*** Dogs are extremely welcome but must be leashed.

item.title: Scenic AVL - Camino Primitivo - with WNC American Pilgrims — Sat Nov 7, 9:00 AM
item.description:
The Asheville Hiking Group **Overview:** This hike is offered as a monthly training hike with the WNC Asheville Chapter of American Pilgrims on the Camino. The route has been announced on the [Facebook Group Page](https://www.facebook.com/groups/AVLCamino/announcements). If you are unfamiliar with the Camino, here are a few links to learn more: [American Pilgrims on the Camino](https://americanpilgrims.org/iwpmap_directory/western-north-carolina/) [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Way_(2010_film)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Way_(2010_film)) This route is inspired by the Camino Primitivo, which has more hills than most of the other routes to Santiago de Compostela.

item.title: Sacred Forests of the World — Sat Nov 7, 1:00 PM
item.description: Sacred Forests of the World with Alison Ormsby Saturday, November 7 | 1 – 3 pm BRN – Elective Register Here! This class will explore the biological and cultural aspects of areas around the world that are conserved due to local beliefs and traditions. Sacred natural sites include forests, mountains, and springs that have cultural significance. Some sites also have taboos on use of species within the areas, which serves a conservation function. Most are not government-protected lands; rather, are managed by local committees, caretakers and/or religious leaders. Specific examples and research from India, Ghana, and Sierra Leone will be shared. Participants will discuss possible connections to forests in Western North Carolina. Alison Ormsby has a PhD in Environmental Studies and is a human ecologist with 30 years of experience working with people and protected areas, environmental education, and sacred natural sites. In this program, we will look closely at the common trees around the NC Arboretum trails and point out specific characteristics of their buds and bark so you can identify them even without their leaves.
